title: Sita changes Rama's mind
hookLine: Rama lists the forest's dangers, Sita answers every one, and he gives way; why devotees say Sita-Ram
carry: Sita-Ram: never one without the other
tomorrow: not everyone is calm. what will Lakshmana say?
last: A PARTNER IN DHARMA SHARES THE ROAD.

cards: How do you stop someone you love from following you into danger, without forbidding it? Rama tries a list: every hardship the forest holds, one by one. It's love, mostly, and also a way of winning without saying no.
He has watched his father break and his mother weep today, and he wants one person he loves kept safe. He means every word. And Sita, who has been patient, runs out of patience.

teach.b: The forest is hard, Rama says. Lions roar from mountain caves. Rivers are full of crocodiles.
You sleep on fallen leaves and eat whatever fruit you find, or nothing. Wind, darkness, hunger, snakes, thorns. Stay here.
Sita answers his list item by item. With you, the grass will feel like a soft blanket; the fruit you bring me will taste like nectar.
And when I was a girl, people who read the signs told my family I would one day live in a forest. Still Rama hesitates, and she stings.

teach.h: A WOMAN IN THE FORM OF A MAN?
teach.b: What was my father thinking, she asks, when he chose as his son-in-law a woman in the form of a man? Valmiki doesn't soften it. She's accusing Rama of failing at the one thing a protector is for: keeping her with him.
Then she weeps. And Rama gives way. He holds her.

teach.h: I DIDN'T KNOW YOUR MIND. COME.
teach.b: I didn't know your mind, he says. I wouldn't want heaven itself without you. Come with me.
In a story about a son obeying his father without a question, the wife questions, pushes, and changes her husband's mind. And this is why, in Hindu devotion, Rama is almost never alone.
Temples and home shrines show Sita beside him.
Devotees chant Sita-Ram, her name first, and many greet each other with Jai Siya Ram. Some traditions teach that you come to God through the Goddess at his side; that's a reading.
The text says it plainer: he didn't want heaven without her.

how: Rama is rarely shown alone: temples and home shrines picture him with Sita, and devotees chant Sita-Ram and greet each other with Jai Siya Ram, her name first.

o: how Sita answers every danger until Rama gives way
how Sita convinces Bharata to refuse the throne
how Sita talks Rama into defying his father

p: said Sita would live in a forest
a woman in the form of a man?
I didn't know your mind; come

s: Rama agrees as soon as Sita asks
he tries a long list of dangers first.
Sita says she was told as a girl she'd live in a forest
and she's wanted to see it ever since.
he keeps her rebuke as it is.

games.q: you're Rama. your wife has answered every danger you named and wept. what do you do?
o: insist she stay; it's for her own good.
send her to her father's house.
admit you didn't know her mind, and take her.
games.why: Rama holds her and says he wouldn't want heaven without her. come with me, he says.

practice: Try a practice many Hindus keep: japa, repeating a holy name. Breathe in, and silently say Sita; breathe out, and say Ram. Let the two names travel together, the way the two of them did.
If you don't pray, breathe in on with, out on together, and think of someone you'd walk a hard road beside.

wordCard.voice: Sita's argument, won. She answers every danger, rebukes Rama sharply, and he relents: I didn't know your mind; come with me.

orig.note: Sanskrit vanavāsa: forest-dwelling, exile in the forest; vana (forest) plus vāsa (living).

carryVoice: Hold on to it: Sita-Ram, never one without the other. Tomorrow, someone in the palace isn't calm at all. That's day five hundred twenty-seven.
